title: Capstone Part 3: Deploy, Monitor, and Document
summary: Part 3 completes your capstone by taking the working build live and wrapping it in the operational and documentation polish that makes it a genuine, portfolio-worthy deliverable - because in the real world an automation is only finished when it runs
content:
# Capstone Part 3: Deploy, Monitor, and Document ##### The last 10% that is 50% of the value Your capstone works. Every fixture passes. On your machine, with test credentials, pointed at a test database, it does exactly what the plan said it would. None of that is worth anything to a business yet. Between "it works in testing" and "it is running the company's actual process" sits a set of activities that beginners skip and professionals treat as the real job: a safe cutover, production monitoring, backups, a maintenance plan, and documentation good enough that someone else can operate it. The Google SRE book (Beyer et al., 2016) makes the point that operating software is a distinct discipline from writing it — and in automation, where your work runs unattended against live business data, that is doubly true. Today you finish. Not "the workflow is done," but "the automation is *in service*." ##### Going live safely: the cutover The riskiest moment in any automation project is the switch to real data. A careful cutover is a sequence, not a switch flip. **1. Pre-flight checklist.** Work through it explicitly: ```text [ ] All production credentials created and stored in the credential manager [ ] Test credentials removed from the production workflow [ ] Environment variables set (URLs, keys, DB connection, timezone) [ ] Production database schema created, with constraints and indexes [ ] Webhook URLs updated to production endpoints (not the test URL!) [ ] Time zone set to Asia/Kolkata everywhere [ ] Notification destinations changed from #bot-testing to real channels [ ] Error alerting configured and TESTED (break something on purpose) [ ] Workflow exported to Git and tagged [ ] Rollback plan written down ``` **2. Shadow run.** Let the automation run against real inputs but with its final actions disabled — write to a shadow table instead of the real one, send emails to yourself instead of customers. Run for a day and compare its output with what the humans did. Any discrepancy is a bug you found for free. **3. Parallel run.** Enable it for real, but keep the manual process going alongside for a few days. Yes, this is duplicated effort. It is also how you build the client's trust and catch the case your fixtures missed. **4. Limited scope first.** Enable for one supplier, one region, or 10% of volume. Watch it. Then widen. **5. Full cutover** with the manual process formally retired — and a **rollback plan**: how do you turn this off and revert to manual within ten minutes if something goes wrong? Write it down before you need it. ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Test env
fixtures] --> B[Shadow run
real input, no real output] B --> C[Parallel run
both automation and human] C --> D[Limited scope
10% of volume] D --> E[Full production] E -.rollback.-> C ``` ##### Deployment, hosting, and scheduling Apply Day 32. The decisions to lock in: **Where it runs.** n8n Cloud, a self-hosted instance on a VPS, or a PaaS. Whatever you choose, it must not be your laptop. **Restart policy.** `restart: unless-stopped` in Docker, or the platform's equivalent, so a crash or a server reboot does not silently end your service. **Environment separation.** Distinct credentials, database and destinations for dev and prod. If you run both on one instance, prefix workflow names and use separate credential entries. **Schedules with correct time zones.** Verify by scheduling a throwaway run five minutes out and confirming it fires when you expect. **Resource headroom.** Check memory and CPU under real load, not fixture load. Browser automation and large payloads are memory-hungry. **Version pinning.** Pin your n8n image tag rather than `latest`, so an unattended pull cannot bring a breaking change overnight. ##### Monitoring, logging, and alerting in production Apply Day 31 concretely. The minimum viable production observability for your capstone: ```sql -- Every run writes one row here CREATE TABLE automation_runs ( id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY, workflow TEXT NOT NULL, run_id TEXT, started_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), duration_ms INT, status TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('success','failed','skipped')), record_key TEXT, items_in INT DEFAULT 0, items_out INT DEFAULT 0, error_code TEXT, error_message TEXT ); -- The health query your daily digest runs SELECT COUNT(*) AS runs_24h, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'success') AS ok, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed') AS failed, ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status='success') / NULLIF(COUNT(*),0), 1) AS success_rate, ROUND(AVG(duration_ms)) AS avg_ms FROM automation_runs WHERE started_at >= now() - interval '24 hours'; ``` Three alerts, at minimum: 1. **Immediate failure alert** — a run failed after exhausting retries. Include the workflow, the record key, the error, and what the system already did about it. 2. **Staleness watchdog** — a scheduled check that alerts if no successful run has occurred within the expected window. This is the one that catches silent death. 3. **Daily health digest** — run count, success rate, failures by type, items processed. Two minutes to read, and it makes trends visible before they become incidents. Then **test the alerts**. Revoke a credential and confirm the message arrives with useful content. An untested alert is a decoration. ##### Backups and a maintenance plan **Backups** cover three things: the workflow definitions (export to Git *and* the platform's own backup), the database (nightly `pg_dump`, shipped offsite), and the encryption key or secrets (stored separately from the server, in a password manager). Then restore from a backup once, in a scratch environment, to prove it works. **A maintenance plan** is what turns a delivered project into a supported one. Write it down: ```markdown ## Maintenance plan — Supplier Confirmation Automation **Owner:** ananya@example.com **Backup owner:** ravi@example.com ### Daily (automated) - Health digest to #ops at 09:00 IST - Failure alerts, real time ### Weekly (5 min, Monday) - Review the review-queue table; reprocess or correct - Check success rate trend and AI extraction accuracy sample ### Monthly (30 min) - Verify a backup restores - Review credential expiry dates and rotate anything ageing - Check API deprecation notices from integrated vendors - Review cost vs budget ### Quarterly - Re-measure success metrics against the Part 1 baseline - Review the phase-2 backlog with the process owner - Update dependencies and the n8n version (staging first) ### Known risks to watch - Supplier email format changes → watch extraction confidence trend - OAuth token expiry on the Gmail connection → alerts on 401 ``` ##### Full documentation and demo Documentation is what makes your capstone a **portfolio piece** rather than a private achievement. Four artefacts: **1. README** — the front door. Purpose, the problem in one paragraph, architecture diagram, tech stack, how to run it, environment variables, and a link to everything else. **2. Architecture diagram** — the Mermaid or drawn diagram showing systems, data flow, decisions, state and error paths. One image that explains the whole thing. **3. Operations and troubleshooting guide** — the document your future replacement needs: ```markdown ## Troubleshooting ### Symptom: no runs in the last 6 hours 1. Is the workflow Active? (n8n → Workflows → toggle) 2. Is the container up? `docker compose ps` 3. Check the Gmail credential — 401s appear in `automation_runs.error_code` 4. Check the inbox filter/label — has anyone changed it? ### Symptom: records piling up in `manual_review` Usually the AI extraction confidence dropped. Check whether a supplier changed their email template; review 10 recent samples and update the prompt examples in the "Extract fields" node. ### Symptom: duplicate rows in purchase_orders Should be impossible (PK on po_number). If seen, check whether someone disabled the ON CONFLICT clause in the upsert node. ``` **4. Before/after impact** — the measured result, which is the part a hiring manager reads first: ```text BEFORE AFTER CHANGE Time per confirmation 22 min 1.8 min -92% Ops hours per month 16.5 h 1.4 h -15.1 h Re-keying errors/month ~3 0 -100% Confirmation lag ~7 h 11 min -97% Monthly running cost — ₹1,050 (₹9,060 net saving) Automation success rate — 98.6% (30-day measured) ``` **The demo** — a 3–5 minute recorded walkthrough. Structure it: the problem (30s), the live automation running end to end (2 min), the architecture and one interesting technical decision (1 min), the measured impact (30s). Loom or OBS is fine. This video will do more for your job search than another certificate. ##### Common pitfalls - **Big-bang cutover** with no shadow or parallel phase. - **Test URLs or credentials** left in the production workflow. - **Alerts configured but never tested.** - **No rollback plan** — panicking is not a plan. - **Backups that have never been restored.** - **No named owner** — an unowned automation rots. - **Documentation written for yourself** rather than a stranger. - **Claiming impact without measurement** — always cite how you measured. - **Declaring done at go-live.** The first week in production teaches you the most. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: **take your capstone live**. Switch to production credentials and triggers with a careful cutover, enable **logging and failure alerts**, set up a **backup** of the workflow and data, and confirm it runs correctly on **real data**. Do the shadow run even if it feels like an unnecessary delay — it is where you will find the case your fixtures missed. The mini project finalizes it as a **portfolio piece**: deployed, monitored, backed up, plus complete documentation (README, architecture diagram, operations and troubleshooting guide, measured before/after impact) and a **short recorded demo**. Push it all to a public repository. This single project, presented well, is stronger evidence than any list of tools on a résumé. For the assignment, write the **results section**: restate the success metrics you defined in Part 1, report the **actual outcome** — time saved, money saved, errors reduced — and describe your **monitoring and maintenance plan**. Be honest about metrics you missed and why. A results section that says "we targeted 3 minutes and achieved 1.8, but AI extraction accuracy came in at 93% against a 95% target, so discrepancies still route to human review" reads as far more credible than uniform success. ##### Key takeaways - Cut over gradually: pre-flight checklist, shadow run, parallel run, limited scope, then full production — with a written rollback plan. - Deploy somewhere that survives reboots, with pinned versions, separated environments, correct time zones and resource headroom. - Production needs a run log, a failure alert, a staleness watchdog and a daily digest — and every alert must be tested by deliberately breaking something. - Back up workflows, database and secrets separately, restore once to prove it, and write a maintenance plan with a named owner and a schedule. - Documentation and a measured before/after are what convert a working automation into a portfolio piece; record a short demo and publish it.
